title: Coral and the Griffin's Gift
markdown:
High in the jagged peaks of the Frostfang Range, stone towers clung to sheer ridges like moss and the wind sang songs older than any village charter. Witch Coral’s home was a tall spiral of grey stone reaching toward swirling cloud, the ravines below filling themselves with shadow. It was a quiet place, far above the busy world. Always by her side: Pepper, no ordinary stoat. His senses could find a dewdrop on a spider’s web at a hundred yards. He understood his witch better than anyone, in a language of shared glances and subtle nudges. In those days witches often kept sleek black cats. Coral and Pepper had not applied for typical.

Coral was peculiar even among witches. She did not cackle or brew smoky noxious pots. Her magic was quiet skill, a gentle nudge at the world’s edges, a gardener coaxing a shy bloom. She made potions that tasted of spiced apple cider and mended broken things with moonlight thread, leaving no seam. Pepper, dark shining fur, bright intelligent eyes, was her constant shadow, a comfort in the mountain emptiness that could otherwise talk too loud.

One crisp morning the pale northern sun warmed frost-stone. “We need a new addition,” Coral said. “A pet, perhaps, for the quiet days.” Pepper paused mid-whisker, nose working, gaze steady.

“The old magic says a familiar must respect you. Not only obey. Respect who you are. Trickier than a truth serum a goblin would swallow. Finding that up here is not like finding a sock.”

They descended icy scree. Hardy goats, sure-footed, more interested in moss than witchly regard. Shy snow hares, white on white, married to speed. “Inspiration,” Coral murmured. “The Oracle of the Gleaming Horn.”

Pepper chittered the translation: Bartholomew.

“His official title, on important days.”

The unicorn’s hidden meadow always seemed to have better sun, impossible flower-colours, air with a gentle tune. Bartholomew himself was exuberant cheer, grin wide, horn pulsing gold. A walking weather of sunshine.

“Greetings, Coral! Little furry one! Quest? Doldrums? Misplaced rainbow?”

“Advice. A companion that will truly respect. The mountain is elusive.”

The horn brightened. “Respect blooms from understanding, and understanding from a path with challenges. Seek the Sky-Whisperers, where griffin chicks learn courage. They respect strength, observation, the quiet of ages.” A spin, glitter Pepper sniffed at with suspicion. “Follow the Whispering Winds past the Three Sisters of Stone. When the moon is high, a bridge of moonlight if you look closely. Easy peasy.”

Coral’s exasperation flickered and was filed. “Moonlight bridge. Sisters. Right.”

“Sparkles and song!” He cantered. The sun sat down.

And so they set out. The Whispering Winds, a mournful sigh, guided them through high passes where the scree remembered every foot. The Three Sisters of Stone, towering granite monoliths, loomed and cast shadows long enough to lose a day in. Dusk settled. Ahead, a soft ethereal glow bloomed that was not entirely a unicorn’s fib.

“He wasn’t entirely making it up,” Coral said, hushed.

Before them, suspended between dizzying ravines, hung a rope that was not hemp or leather. It seemed woven of moonlight: silver strands shimmering and shifting, each pulsing a gentle lamp. The wind tugged. The span swayed over a dark that did not explain itself, a daunting ribbon against deepening twilight, shy stars beginning to take their places.

Pepper, usually bold, flattened against her boot, sleek body vibrating. She tested the first moon-strand. Cool, surprisingly solid. She stepped, movements deliberate. The howl tried to buffet them into the chasm. Coral moved with an inner stillness the storm found expensive, drawing something from the mountain that was not a shouted spell. Pepper, seeing the resolve, found his own courage and his claws, dark fur a contrast on the luminous weave. Breathless, they reached the far stone, hearts doing a louder job than usual.

The far alcove held no dragons. Two fluffy griffin chicks chirped. The bolder one assessed them with a sharp intelligent eye.

Coral knelt, no food, no bargain. She spoke low, of mountain patience, of stone that endures, of life that stays in harsh places. She did not demand.

The chick — Spark, she named it inwardly — watched her hands, the calm, the stoat who had crossed. Then a soft chirp, a downy head against her palm. A choice offered, not taken.

Pepper’s whiskers approved.

They returned from the peaks soon after, Coral carrying Spark carefully, the young griffin nestled against her cloak, a picture of trust. As they neared Oakhaven the air warmed, roasting roots and woodsmoke. Hardy folk celebrated good fortune; a witch with a new wild friend was cause enough for tables. Lanterns on cobbles. Crusty bread, rich stew, sweet berry tarts. Children gathered to gaze; Spark chirped from her shoulder, sharp eyes taking inventory. Pepper sat regal. Coral accepted greetings with quiet grace and a rare genuine smile.

A small child offered Spark a sliver of apple. Coral did not lecture the square about desire, patience, or being true. She let Spark decide about the fruit, paid for two tarts, and started the long walk back to the spiral while the lanterns were still honest. Behind them the moonlight bridge went back to being wind. Bartholomew, had anyone asked, would have called it sparkles and song. Pepper, who had crossed it, called it a bridge, and went to sleep on the hearth like a comma at the end of a long sentence.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
